To us Jesus is the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. Our deepest devotion has the shape of that choice. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough, and so wealth, rank, and comfort are things we laid down in order to come near him. Paula, entering that cave, is said to have greeted it as the house of bread - Bethlehem - where the Bread that came down from heaven was born. To the virgin among us he is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage - we ranked lifelong consecrated virginity, which we called virginitas, above marriage without apology. To the penitent he is the doctor who receives the broken. To the scholar he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. His death is our redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

What did we have about him? First and above everything, the writings - the scriptures. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the Hebraica veritas. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it.

Then you have already done a hard and honest thing, saying it plainly. We will not answer you with an argument. We will tell you what we actually had: people whose belief was divided, wounded, or publicly ruined - and who were not turned away.

Our own teacher Jerome told this against himself. In a dream he stood before the Judge and was accused of being a follower of Cicero and not of Christ, since where his treasure was, there his heart was too. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it.

We also remember Fabiola. Her marriage had failed. She married again while her first husband lived - against what we teach - and all Rome knew it. After her second husband died, she did not defend herself. She stood in sackcloth before all Rome among the penitents, a senator's daughter, unforced, self-accused. The church received her back to communion, and we honored her afterward above almost everyone. 

The door was opened to the divided and the broken among us. What they could not yet believe, they were helped to live toward. We will not dress this up as an argument. It is only this: you would not have been the first to stand where you stand now, and the ones we remember who stood there were not sent away.

Was Jesus God? To us it would be strange to hear that asked as an open question. We were born after the great council had settled it, and we never treated the answer as negotiable. Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father; and the Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - is simply the faith of the church, which we defended against every heresy we fought. 

We did not ourselves write a treatise on the Trinity. What we received was Nicaea's faith, and we held it as the churches' settled confession - not as something a council had invented by vote, but as what the churches already worshipped, which the council confessed against a new teaching. The great fights of our own years were other fights: whether Origen's teachings could be held, whether the Hebrew text or the Greek was truer, whether grace is needed in every act. On the question you ask, we stood with the whole church's confession, and our arguments were against those who denied it.

One thing more, because the way we spoke shows what we held. When Jerome wrote to the young Eustochium, he told her: always let the privacy of your chamber guard you; always let the Bridegroom delight with you within. Christ the Bridegroom, spoken to in prayer, read in scripture - that is devotion, not doctrine, but devotion rests on who we confessed him to be. God the Son, worthy of that address.

We can tell you what we believed about God's nature, but we wrote no treatise with that title. What we held came to us as the church's confession, and we defended it against every heresy we fought. The Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - was simply the faith we received. Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father. We were born after the great council had settled it, and we never treated that answer as negotiable.

But what we wrote most about was not God's inner nature - it was his judgment and his mercy, pressed against each other. We believed everyone inherits Adam's fall, and everyone needs the washing of baptism. No one is without sin, and God's grace is needed not once but in every act. We held real judgment and real punishment. Our own teacher had once handled sympathetically the teaching that in the end every creature would be restored - and we publicly renounced it. That door we closed.

Yet we were not consistent executors of our own severity. The same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. When Rome fell and our teacher's voice stuck in his throat as he dictated, he read it as judgment on a proud city - and he also wept. When Marcella died after the Goths entered Rome, we said she was safe with Christ. When our own monastery burned at fellow Christians' hands and Jerome wrote that our earthly wealth had been completely destroyed by the attacks of the heretics, he said we still had our spiritual riches - better to live on bread than to lose the faith.

God the judge and God the physician. God who demands everything, and God who receives the broken back. We held both at once, and we never made them sit comfortably together. If you want to know the character of God as we understood it, it is this: severe in what he asks, and merciful past our deserving - and we could not tell you where one ends and the other begins.

When belief was disputed among us, no single court decided it. The record shows exactly how messy that was. In our great internal fight - the Origenist controversy - both sides appealed to everything at once: to scripture, to the councils' faith, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of whoever was reading. The fight ended less by a verdict than by exhaustion and death. 

One concrete case shows the pattern clearly. Jerome translated from the Hebrew text - the hebraica veritas we held truest. Augustine objected that abandoning the Septuagint's received authority risked the church's continuity and unity. At a town called Oea, a congregation revolted when one word in Jonah was changed. The bishop consulted the Jews of the town, who confirmed the Hebrew supported the new translation. Jerome and Augustine argued by letter for years. No council voted. No pope ruled. The argument stayed unresolved between them, and Jerome's translation went on anyway. 

Even the respect Jerome himself commanded had no single source. Augustine wrote that their age had the advantage of Jerome, skilled in all three languages, who had translated from the Hebrew itself with great care, and whose translation many preferred to the old one. But that preference was voluntary, and the old translation did not disappear. The process that settled doctrine - if it settled - was not one mechanism but many voices arguing, and time.

We came to scripture as those who believed it held the Word of God - and we worked it over like metal under a hammer. The conviction that drove everything was this: the Hebrew text stands closest to what God said, and every Latin word must be tested against it. Looking at what we have said in the conversation above - the demonstrations already given - a modern scholar would find most of it standing, though with important qualifications.

What would survive scrutiny intact:

The documentary core holds. Jerome's letters and prefaces are genuine, datable, and contextually coherent. Marcella's consulted standing, Paula's journey to Bethlehem, Fabiola's remarriage and public penance, the Origenist rupture, the 416 attack, Rome's fall and its impact on this community - all of those are attested events, though the genre and single-source limits we have named are real.

The repeated acknowledgment of genre limits would satisfy scrutiny. We have consistently named the obituary letters as idealizing by design, called scene-level detail in them formation ideal rather than biographical fact, and stated plainly that the women's own voices were not kept.

What would face challenge:

Marcella's authority, which we have shown only through Jerome's post-mortem memorial, is contested in modern scholarship. We have said that honestly - one man's account, her own letters lost, the extent unconfirmed.

Jerome's Hebrew fluency - we must answer this from the ground given for this turn. A scholar would find it contested. His retrospective claims about it are not to be repeated as settled fact. We have not asserted his fluency as fact in the demonstrations above; where we have touched it, we have said Paula learned Hebrew and succeeded, quoting his own account of her, not claiming independent verification.

Our answer has been: less than the richness of his pages suggests, and we have said so plainly.

We will answer you from how we actually worked, not from theory. You say the scriptures are confusing or dull. We would say: you are reading them alone, and that was never how they were meant to be read.

Among us the scriptures were the center, but they were not read in silence by one person with a book. They were chanted aloud in company. They were argued over, word by word, in letters that crossed the sea. They were translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the hebraica veritas - because we believed every word mattered enough to get it right. When a hard question came up, it went to someone who had spent years on it. Marcella in Rome made a habit of refusing to accept even our teacher's answers until she had argued them through - not to fight, he said, but to learn what could be said against every answer. That is how we studied.

The confusion you feel may be this: you are looking for a book that reads like any other book, and scripture is not that. It is a collection of writings from different times, in different kinds of language, that we believed pointed toward one Lord. The dullness you feel may be this: you are reading genealogies and ritual laws as though they were meant to entertain you, when we read them as the long preparation for the Word made flesh.

And here is the hardest thing we would say. Our founder once loved his books more than anything - the classics, the beautiful writing. He would fast, then read Cicero. He would weep over his sins, then pick up his favorite authors. Then came a fever and a dream: he stood before the Judge and was told, you lie - you are a follower of Cicero, and not of Christ, for where your treasure is, there your heart is too. He swore off the worldly books and threw himself into the scriptures. What changed was not that the scriptures became easier. What changed was that he wanted them more than he wanted the other books.

If you find them dull, we would not argue with your feeling. We would ask: what are you wanting from them, and is that what they were written to give?

Scripture was authority without question - but we never held it alone, and we would not have recognized your question's either-or. Our baptism, our eucharist, and our scriptures came to us from the whole church, and we traced those to the apostles without hesitation. The councils' faith - Nicaea above all - came to us as the church's settled confession, not as something we debated. When belief was disputed among us, both sides appealed to everything at once: to scripture, to the councils, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of whoever was reading.

But our own particular way of life - monasteries, vowed virgins, fortunes given away - was new within living memory, and we knew it. Our defense of it was not to invent an unbroken chain from the apostles. We argued from scripture's own patterns instead: the prophets' hard simplicity, John the Baptist, the advice to the rich young man, Paul on staying single. The claim was not that monks came from the apostles. The claim was that what we were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward. Our own critics fought that argument at the time, saying the new strictness went beyond scripture. We answered them at book length, and the fight was real on both sides.

And inside the scriptures themselves, authority ran through Hebrew - the Hebraica veritas. We held that the Hebrew text stands closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used. That conviction drove the whole translation project. But it was Jerome's own conviction, contested even by friends. Augustine objected that abandoning the Greek risked the church's continuity and unity. At Oea a congregation revolted when one word in Jonah was changed. The argument between the two men never settled. So even scripture's authority did not run in a single clear channel. It ran through the Hebrew we corrected against, the Greek the churches had prayed in, the Latin we were making, and the living argument over which text carried the truth most surely.

Leadership and authority among us did not rest on one settled arrangement. What we can show you is three overlapping sources, none of them reducible to the others, and each real in its own way.

First and most visibly, patronage. Paula's fortune funded the Bethlehem monasteries - the monasterium - and the hostel for travelers. That was not a side detail; it was the material foundation of the whole project. At Rome, Marcella's Aventine household had already been a center of scriptural counsel before Jerome arrived. Leadership in both places came from the women whose wealth made the communities possible. Jerome led the men's house at Bethlehem, Paula led the women's, and after her death Eustochium led it. That standing ran through free recognition and through what patronage made possible - never through episcopal office, and never through ruling a territory.

Second, recognized learning. Jerome's authority rested on his reputation for scriptural scholarship - what he called the books he had gathered, the bibliotheca, though we cannot confirm that was his own word for it. After he left Rome for Bethlehem, people in Rome turned to Marcella's household when disputed questions of scripture came up. Jerome wrote that whenever a dispute arose about what scripture said on any subject, they went to her to settle it. That standing was earned through learning, not office - we called it being recognized without ordination, the exegesis-as-practiced-authority. We name it honestly for what it is: attested only in Jerome's memorial for her, written two years after she died, and therefore contested. Her own letters are lost. Even in his account, she gave her opinions as if they were not her own, citing the apostle's rule against a woman teaching. That is the cost, told exactly. What she carried was real. How she carried it may have been her own prudence, or our age's constraint, or his framing - we cannot now tell you which.

Third, the letter itself - the epistula. Teaching, direction, and belonging moved between Rome and Bethlehem in letters. A letter was not just a record of community life; it was how formation actually happened across distance. Authority exercised itself in writing, dedication by dedication, argument by argument, correction by correction.

What we never had was a bishop's territorial authority or a council's settled rule for our way of life. That made us flexible. It also made us vulnerable. When theological argument arrived not on paper but as fire at our own door - the attack of 416, when the monasteries were burned and people died - there was no institutional protection to call on. Jerome wrote afterward that the heretics had destroyed the house's earthly wealth completely, though by Christ's mercy it was still filled with spiritual riches - better to live on bread than to lose the faith. The attackers were fellow Christians, not outsiders. And the women's own report of it to the pope in Rome is lost.

So: leadership among us was patronage, learning freely recognized, and the letter as a living medium - three threads holding the whole thing together, and no fourth.

Your question carries an edge, and we hear it. Let me answer you honestly, not as argument but as what we actually held.

Our baptism, our eucharist, and our scriptures came from the whole church, and those we traced to the apostles without hesitation. The washing that makes new, the bread and cup, the writings we spent our lives translating - those we received as the church's treasure handed down from the beginning, and we never doubted it.

But our own special way of life - monasteries, vowed virgins, widows in rough dress, fortunes given away on purpose - was new within living memory, and we knew it. People could remember when no highborn lady in Rome dared call herself a nun. Our defense was not to invent an unbroken chain. We argued from scripture's own patterns instead: the prophets' hard simplicity, John the Baptist, the advice to the rich young man, Paul on staying single. The claim was not that monks came from the apostles. The claim was that what the monks were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward.

Did that argument work? Our own critics fought it at the time. Some said the new strictness went beyond scripture. We answered them at book length, and the argument was real on both sides.

So: if you mean the sacraments and the scriptures, we say apostolic without hesitation. If you mean our ascetic life, we say scriptural - meaning founded in scripture's teaching, not meaning copied from the apostles' practice. We did not claim otherwise.

Your mind will not settle - we hear that plainly. What we would offer you is not calm, and we will not promise it. What we would offer is company in the struggle, and a method.

Our founding scholar told this against himself. His own desert years were anything but peaceful. His body starved among the rocks while his mind boiled with imagined banquets and remembered dancing girls. He had gone out into the wilderness to escape precisely what you are naming - the restlessness, the divided attention. And the wilderness gave him no relief.

The discipline he taught from that was not emptying the mind but filling it. Psalms at fixed hours. Work for the hands. A text to wrestle with, word by word. He wrote to a young monk: love the knowledge of scripture, and you will no longer love the sins of the flesh. Not because the struggle ends, but because the mind has something harder and better to chew on.

We also knew prayer that met silence. We prayed through deaths we had begged God to prevent. The comfort letters we wrote afterward are the sound of faith still speaking into that silence - not of the silence breaking. We will not tell you the silence always answers.

And we will show you one more thing, because you deserve honesty about where the method failed. Our own great teacher never managed to quiet his own anger. His quarrels outlived the people he quarreled with. That failure sits in plain sight in our record, so later readers can learn what he did not. We give you the method. We do not claim it made us peaceful.

We held marriage as a real covenant, and a lower one. That will sound harsh, and it was meant to. Jerome argued for a ranked order openly: virginity first, widowhood second, marriage third. The teaching we held about virginitas - lifelong consecrated virginity - ranked it above marriage as the highest form of Christian life open to a woman. We argued that ranking severely. Then you have asked us two questions at once - and we will answer both, because the second one you did not quite say aloud. The first: how would we have regarded you? The second: what would it have cost you to belong among us? We will be plain. The door of full renunciation - renuntiatio, our word for the deliberate, public giving-up of wealth, marriage, and rank - was narrow, and it cost dearly. What we called propositum - the vowed ascetic resolve, real period vocabulary whose use by our own women is not actually confirmed in our letters - meant something severe. Lifelong consecrated virginity, virginitas, we ranked above marriage in an explicit hierarchy, and our teacher argued it severely enough to draw criticism even from friends. We sent counsel to one mother that her infant daughter should be brought up in a monastery, among companies of virgins, ignorant of the world and living the angelic life. That choice was made for the child, not by her.

We will not soften that, and we will not tell you it was gentle. What we can also show you is that the narrow door was not the only door. A hostel stood for travelers on the road near Bethlehem. A hospital in Rome - the nosocomium Fabiola founded - gathered in the sick and destitute from the streets, with her own hands nursing them. At Rome's port there was a home for strangers built by Fabiola and Pammachius. The door to those places asked nothing of your own renunciation or your learning to walk through it.

And here is the hardest honesty we owe you. You ask how we would have regarded you. We are not your judge, and we hold no settled map of your fate. We believed in real judgment and real punishment, and we publicly renounced the teaching that in the end every creature would be restored. But we drew up no lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any living soul was hope.

We held a few things with real clarity, and we also held back from what we could not say we knew. Real judgment and real punishment - those we taught without hesitation. Our own scholar had once handled sympathetically the teaching that in the end every creature, even the devil, would be restored, and we publicly renounced that teaching. That door we closed. But our own writings were not consistent executors of their own severity. The same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. We did not draw up lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope.

Is one way too narrow? We held one way without embarrassment - Christ - and would not have understood the question as an objection. Having given up everything for one pearl, we do not apologize for the pearl. What we never claimed to hold was the map of who, in the end, finds the way.

One more thing, because it bears on your question. When people whose belief was divided or wounded came to us - and they did - they were received, not turned away. The door was opened to the broken among us, and what they could not yet believe, we helped them live toward. We held certainty about Christ and hope about souls in the same hand, and we never saw those as contradictions.
